planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in well-drained, humus-rich soil in shade; in zone 9 plant September–March. Growth is slow, so set plants closer together than typical sedges for quicker coverage.

directions: Plant in dry to medium-moist, acidic to circumneutral woodland soil in partial to full shade; this diminutive native forms tight, wiry tufts of glossy dark green foliage that stay evergreen through mild winters. It is unusually tolerant of the dry, root-filled soil beneath mature oaks and hickories, making it a good small-scale substitute for grass in shaded beds where taller sedges would look out of scale. Growth is slow and clump-forming rather than spreading, so it works best massed in drifts or tucked among stepping stones. Established plants need little care beyond an occasional light grooming of old foliage in late winter.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in consistently moist soil near a shaded seep or stream margin; keep newly set plants well watered until established, since this species does not tolerate drought.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, sandy or acidic soil in partial to full shade, ideally near a seep, spring, or streambank where its natural habitat is mimicked. Bent sedge forms loose, arching tufts of glossy green leaves and takes its name from the gently bent beak of its seed capsules, a feature more relevant to identification than to garden display. It spreads gradually by short rhizomes into a soft-textured colony, making it a good choice for naturalizing along the damp margins of a shaded rain garden or woodland path in the Gulf South. Unlike drought-tolerant upland sedges, it performs poorly if the soil is allowed to dry out for extended periods.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in wet to consistently moist soil in shade; tolerates occasional standing water once established, making it useful along the edges of a rain garden or shaded pond.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, such as a bottomland woodland edge, shaded rain garden, or the damp margin of a pond. Thicket sedge produces reddish-based, three-angled stems and long, drooping, blue-green leaves that often exceed the flowering culms in length, giving the clump a graceful, cascading look distinct from most upright woodland sedges. It tolerates periodic flooding and heavy clay better than many shade sedges, making it useful in low spots where other groundcovers struggle. Clumps increase slowly and combine well with ferns and other moisture-loving shade perennials.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring in average to moist, well-drained soil in shade; give plants ample room, since this selection spreads into a broad mounding patch several feet wide over a few growing seasons.

directions: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in average to consistently moist soil in partial to full shade; this recent selection of the southeastern native Carex basiantha was collected in South Carolina and introduced by Plant Delights Nursery for its exceptionally fine, weeping texture. It forms a low, dense, evergreen to semi-evergreen tussock that spreads slowly outward into a broad, mounding patch over several growing seasons, reportedly reaching roughly a foot tall and several feet wide with age. Its wide native range from the Carolinas west to Texas suggests good adaptability to Gulf South heat and humidity, though as a newer introduction its long-term garden performance is still being documented. Site it where its wide eventual spread has room to develop without crowding neighboring perennials.
sources: Plant Delights Nursery / Juniper Level Botanic Garden
Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich soil in shade; performs best where soil stays evenly moist through the summer, such as a bottomland or streamside planting.

directions: Plant in moist to seasonally wet, humus-rich soil in partial to full shade, such as a bottomland forest edge or the shaded, calcareous soil found along many Gulf South stream terraces. Sharp-scaled sedge forms dense tufts of flat, hairy-margined leaves on dark maroon-based stems, with flowering culms that rise well above the foliage in spring. It is naturally found in floodplain and bottomland forests from Virginia to Texas and Florida, indicating good heat and humidity tolerance for southern gardens. Use it as a textured filler among taller wetland-edge shrubs or combine it with other native sedges for a naturalistic, layered woodland floor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade; well suited to the damp, low spots of a rain garden or drainage swale that stay saturated after rain.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, humus-rich soil in partial shade to full shade, along the edges of a rain garden, drainage swale, or shaded low spot that stays damp through the growing season. Carolina sedge forms a spreading clump of broad, keeled leaves and triangular stems, tolerating periodic inundation as well as the heavy clay soils common in bottomland forests and roadside ditches across its native range from New Jersey to Texas. It is somewhat coarser in texture than many fine-leaved ornamental sedges, making it a good choice where a bolder, more naturalistic look is wanted at a pond or stream margin. Established colonies need minimal care and help stabilize moist, shaded soil against erosion.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in evenly moist, neutral to alkaline soil in partial to medium shade; best sited in a cooler, sheltered microclimate within warmer zone 8-9 gardens.

directions: Plant in evenly moist, humus-rich, neutral to alkaline soil in partial shade to medium shade, ideally in a woodland setting with limestone-derived or otherwise calcareous soil. Rich woods sedge forms modest, upright tufts of narrow leaves shorter than or equal to its flowering stems, blending unobtrusively into the woodland floor rather than serving as a bold accent. It is native to rich, mesic hardwood forests over high-pH bedrock and is less heat-tolerant than many southeastern sedges, so it is best suited to the cooler, more sheltered microclimates within a warm-zone garden rather than open, exposed beds. Combine it with other calciphile woodland natives such as trilliums or wild gingers for an authentic rich-woods planting.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall in wet to consistently moist soil in partial shade; tolerates shallow standing water and also performs well in more sun than most sedges on this list.

directions: Plant in consistently moist to wet soil in partial shade to full shade, such as a bottomland swamp margin, rain garden, or the shallow standing water at a pond edge. Joor's sedge is an upright, clump-forming species with tall, sharply angled stems and, unusually among garden sedges, flowers later in summer than most Carex, adding textural interest into the warm months. Native to swampy bottomlands across the southeastern United States, it tolerates both standing water and considerable shade, and performs equally well in more sun, giving it flexibility in Gulf South landscapes with variable light. Site it away from more aggressive spreading wetland plants, which can crowd out its slower-expanding clumps.
sources: Mt. Cuba Center — Carex Trial for the Mid-Atlantic Region
